title: Taking up string bass with Streeman and the career timeline
summary: In 1937 the Streeman bassist quit and Al suggested Bob switch; he recounts brokerage day jobs, Navy years, return to Streeman 1947-56, Girard, and Al Hirt.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: How did you get interested in bass by the way?

Well I always did like bass. I always did like string bass, Dick. And around 1937 after playing the guitar for four years in the band I decided, well you know the bass player with the Al Streaming Band who was the vice president of the Soil Company and had to do all that road traveling. He was told Streaming and he said, Al I'm going to have to quit the band. He said, I got too much traveling. He had been with the band ten years. So he left the band and that's when Al told me, he said, Bob why don't you switch over to bass? I know you just recently bought one and you've been working out at the house with it. And because when I bought the guitar I didn't know whether to buy a bass or a guitar. So I bought the guitar and I said, well maybe later on if I still like bass I'll get me a string bass. So four years later in 1937, an early 37, because I already had the bass when I got married in October. So it must have been an early 37 and I bought the string bass at Whirlands. And I bought this bass method book and taught myself as much as I could about it and still be able to work in the daytime, which I was still in those brokerage houses. See I went to work in my first brokerage house in 1928 and I spent seven years with them. And they, they were John F. Clark and Company and they consolidated with the E.A. Pearson Company. And the E.A. Pearson Company consolidated with Fenner and Bean. Then Fenner and Bean consolidated with Merrill Lynch, Pierce Fenner, Ungolight and Smith and all that business, which is now your Merrill Lynch, you know, the big deal. But anyway, I left after, now we're strictly talking about the day job. After seven years with Clark, we went over to Fenner and Bean. I was with Fenner and Bean, excuse me, with Fenner and Bean over a few years when I decided to take a government examination. So I took about six government examinations, some that I wasn't even qualified to take. And I passed three or four of them. And then I got a government offer and that's when I went to work for the War Department down to the Port of Embarcation. And I was there one year when Pearl Harbor came along and then three months to the day after Pearl Harbor, I joined the Navy, stayed in the Navy five years. And I didn't play music for five years, Dick. I could have joined the Navy as a musician, but I'd been playing music and working in the day for thirteen years and I figured I'm going to give it a rest for a while. I played four or five times during that five years up in the US. So that's about the only time I played music. And I think we had a few jam sessions at guys' houses, you know. So if I played ten times in five years, I played plenty, you know. And then after I got out of the Navy in 47, I was streaming, held my job open for a while. So I went back. He had used a lot of substitutes. And I went back with Al. And I stayed with Al from 47 to 56. And in 53, I went with Gerard and the famous Doe, but I worked there three nights a week and worked with Streaming three nights a week. Until 56 when Al Hurts says, Bob, why don't you quit your day job and come work with me? And that brings that up to date then.
But why does Treeman want you on bass? Do you know?
